opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. This is one of the questions that really fascinates me, because it gets at something deep about the gap between what humans do effortlessly and what's so hard for robots.

Think about pushing an object across a table, say a coffee mug or a bottle. You'd think physics would let us predict exactly where it goes. But the motion depends on the friction distribution between the bottom of the object and the surface, and that depends on microscopic details: tiny bumps, dust, a little moisture, slight variations in the material. You can't see any of that, and it changes from moment to moment. So even if you push the same object the same way twice, it can end up in different places. Matt Mason, my PhD advisor at Carnegie Mellon, did foundational work on the mechanics of pushing and showed how fundamentally indeterminate this is.

So how do humans pick things up so reliably despite all that uncertainty? I think the answer is that we don't predict precisely. We use strategies that are robust to what we don't know. When you reach for a glass, you don't calculate its exact position and the exact forces. You approach it in a way that works across a wide range of possibilities. Your hand closes, and as your fingers make contact, the object tends to get pushed into a stable position between them. The uncertainty gets funneled away by the geometry of the grasp itself.

Early in my career I worked on what we called sensorless or "open-loop" manipulation. We showed that for certain parts you could design a sequence of squeezes with a simple parallel-jaw gripper that would orient the part correctly no matter how it started, without any sensing. The idea is that you don't need to know the exact state if the actions are designed to collapse the uncertainty.

And I think that's a lesson for robotics more broadly. A lot of people assume the path forward is better and better models, more precise simulation, perfect perception. Those help, but the real world always has residual uncertainty you can't eliminate. Humans are good at this not because we're perfect predictors, but because over millions of years of evolution and years of childhood play we've learned strategies that are forgiving of error. We use compliance, we use feedback from touch, we make small corrections constantly without being aware of it.

That's also why I'm a bit skeptical when people say robots will soon match human dexterity across the board. Picking up an arbitrary object in a cluttered, unstructured environment, like a messy home, is still extremely difficult. We've made real progress. Our work on Dex-Net, for example, used large amounts of synthetic data to train robots to find grasps that are robust to uncertainty in perception and physics, and that's led to systems that work well in settings like warehouse bin picking. But general-purpose manipulation at the level of a human, or even a small child, is still a grand challenge. I sometimes call it Moravec's paradox in action: the things we find easiest, like picking up a cup, turn out to be the hardest to engineer.

r001.rationale: The response says an object's motion depends on microscopic friction details such as tiny bumps, dust, and moisture, making repeated pushes unpredictable.

r002.rationale: It explains that people avoid needing precise predictions by closing their fingers around an object, which moves it toward a stable position and funnels away uncertainty.

r003.rationale: The response does not define caging as preventing escape while allowing the object freedom to move within an enclosure.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, this is one of my favorite puzzles, because it goes right to the heart of how little we actually understand about physical interaction. We did an experiment in my lab years ago where we took a very simple object, a flat shape, and pushed it across a table with a robot finger. Same object, same table, same push, as controlled as we could make it. And the object ended up in a different place every time. Not wildly different, but different enough that you could never predict exactly where it would land. And that's a flat object on a flat surface, which is about the simplest case you can imagine.

So the question becomes: how is it that humans pick up thousands of objects a day and almost never think about it? You reach for your coffee cup while looking at your phone, and you get it. And I think the answer is that we don't actually predict exactly what's going to happen. We've learned, through a lifetime of trial and error, strategies that are robust to that uncertainty. You cage the object with your hand so that wherever it slides within some range, you still end up with it. You use compliance in your fingers so small errors get absorbed rather than amplified. You get feedback as you go and adjust. You're not solving the physics; you're sidestepping it.

And that's really the shift that happened in robotics. For a long time we tried to model everything, friction coefficients, mass distributions, contact mechanics, and then compute the perfect grasp. And it works in simulation and falls apart on a real table because the friction isn't uniform, there's a bit of dust, the object isn't quite what the CAD model says. What we did with Dex-Net was to flip it around and say, let's not look for the one optimal grasp. Let's look for grasps that still work even if we're wrong about the object's position and shape by some amount. We sample millions of grasps on thousands of objects, perturb them, and keep the ones that survive the perturbation. That's robustness as the objective rather than precision.

I like to call this the gap between control and uncertainty. Nature doesn't give you precise predictions, so nature builds systems that don't need them. And frankly, I think humility about that gap is healthy. Every time someone tells me robots are about to replace all manual labor, I think about that little flat object skidding to a slightly different spot for the hundredth time. We're making progress, real progress, but the physical world keeps reminding us it's more subtle than we'd like.

r001.rationale: The response describes unpredictable outcomes and mentions uneven friction and dust as practical complications, but it does not attribute the unpredictability to nearly submicroscopic frictional interactions.

r002.rationale: It says people use strategies robust to uncertainty, including caging the object with a hand so it can slide within a range and still be captured.

r003.rationale: The response describes caging the object so it can move within a range while remaining captured, which conveys freedom to move within a containing hand enclosure without escaping.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s remarkable is that we don’t need to predict the motion exactly. Imagine picking up a coffee cup: you reach toward it, make contact, and adjust. If it starts to slip, you change your grip. You’re getting information as you act, through vision and touch.

So it’s less like calculating a perfect trajectory in advance and more like a continuous conversation with the physical world. There’s uncertainty about the friction, the weight, and exactly where the contact points are, but you can still choose actions that work across a range of possibilities. That’s a very useful way to think about robotic grasping, too: how can we act reliably even when our model of the world is imperfect?

r001.rationale: It mentions uncertainty about friction, but does not attribute prediction difficulty to nearly submicroscopic frictional interactions.

r002.rationale: It describes adjusting a grip if the cup slips, but does not say people compensate by caging the object with their fingers.

r003.rationale: It does not define caging or describe enclosing an object that can still move within the enclosure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s remarkable is that we don’t need to predict exactly what’s going to happen. If you reach for a coffee cup and it moves a little differently than you expected, you adjust. You’re getting visual information, you’re getting tactile information, and you’re continually correcting your motion.

In robotics, we call this closed-loop control. Rather than computing a perfect plan and then executing it blindly, you act, observe what happened, and act again. You can also choose actions that make the uncertainty less important. If you slide an object up against a wall, for example, you may end up knowing more about where it is than you did before you pushed it.

So the challenge isn’t necessarily to predict every detail of the physics. It’s to find ways of acting that work reliably even when your predictions are imperfect.

r001.rationale: The candidate says exact prediction is unnecessary and refers to imperfect physics predictions, but does not attribute the unpredictability to nearly submicroscopic frictional interactions.

r002.rationale: It describes adjusting motion using visual and tactile feedback and sliding an object against a wall, but does not say people compensate by caging objects with their fingers.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not define caging or describe enclosing an object while allowing it freedom to move within the enclosure.
